segments.text: You've probably seen plenty of headlines about how AI is going to either save the world
or ruin it.
But looking at it strictly as helpful or harmful leaves a massive blind spot.
What exactly are we missing?
Answering that is incredibly difficult.
So to figure it out, we actually need to look at a city that paid people to catch rats.
Specifically Hanoi back in 1902.
The city was facing a severe public health crisis.
Their brand new state-of-the-art sewer system had become a massive breeding ground for thousands
of rats.
To understand why predicting the future of AI is nearly impossible, we first have to see
what happens when human nature meets a flawlessly designed, perfectly logical system.
The colonial government devised a plan that looked brilliant on paper.
They offered a cash bounty to citizens for every severed rat tail turned into the authorities.
Initially, the program looked like a massive success.
The primary metric, the number of tails collected, shot up with tails pouring in by the thousands.
But then, residents spotted something strange.
Rats running around the city streets completely healthy and missing their tails.
It turns out there was a biological flaw in the plan.
Rats don't actually need their tails to survive.
They can live perfectly full lives and, more importantly, keep reproducing without them.
The rat catchers realized this immediately.
Instead of killing their catch, they simply clipped the tails for the bounty and released
the animals back into the sewers to ensure the rat supply stayed strong.
A dead rat pays once.
A live rat pays forever.
Some entrepreneurial citizens took this logic even further.
They bypassed the dangerous sewers entirely and set up dedicated rat farms to harvest tails at scale.
By the time the city finally realized what was happening and scrapped the program,
they were left with a massive mountain of severed tails,
but a rat population that had actually grown larger than before.
The payment system worked exactly as designed.
But the real goal was fewer rats.
And the program encouraged people to keep rats alive.
When a metric doesn't perfectly align with the intended outcome,
people will always optimize for the reward.
The system gets played and the original purpose completely unravels.
This dynamic isn't limited to a 1902 public health policy.
It is a recurring pattern across all of modern history,
where the creators of a new system fail to predict how people will actually use it.
Take a look at this infographic comparing expectations with reality.
In 1995, critics doubted online shopping.
Today, it's a daily habit.
In 1940, Henry Ford predicted flying cars.
Yet we rely on roads.
SMS creators didn't expect texting to dominate.
An imported cane toads spread and poisoned wildlife.
Whether it's economics, software design, transportation or biology,
the initial expectations of the creators almost never match the chaotic reality
of human and natural adoption.
Which brings us right back to the technology sitting in front of us today.
Artificial intelligence.
What might people do with AI that neither the optimists nor the warriors are predicting?
Given our track record, the most impactful thing AI does in your lifetime,
whether it's highly beneficial or deeply disruptive,
is likely going to be something nobody in any lab, startup or academic course
has even thought of yet.
That inherent unpredictability shouldn't make you fear the future.
Rather, it is a critical reason to keep your eyes open and stay alert.
You don't have to perfectly forecast where the tech is going.
Instead, acknowledge the uncertainty.
Watch how everyday people are actually interacting with these tools.
And focus on building adaptable skills that hold their value even when the forecast changes.
As this final note reminds us, some of the biggest results are the ones nobody predicted.
That's the best reason to stay curious.
